newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Finland joins EU's ERM currency grid.
newsitem.headline: Finland joins EU's ERM currency grid.

text.p: Finland joined the European Union's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) currency grid on Saturday in a move hailed as a boost for the prospects of a single European currency.
The EU's monetary committee brought the markka into the grid at a central rate of 3.04 to the German mark, a decision which takes effect on Monday.
The move reflects the determination of Finland, which became a member of the EU less than two years ago, to be among the first group of countries to join economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

It also underlines the strong recovery and increased stability of the Finnish economy, which suffered a deep economic crisis in the early 1990s following the collapse of neighbouring Soviet Union, an important export market for Finland.
The link of the markka to the ERM, which limits fluctuations between participating currencies, was welcomed around the EU.

"The ministers, the governors, the (European) Commission, and the European Monetary Institute warmly welcome the participation of the markka in the exchange rate mechanism, which strengthens the European Monetary System," the monetary committee said in a statement.
"They congratulated the Finnish authorities on the substantial adjustments already achieved by the Finnish economy which is reflected in this decision," it added.
By joining the ERM, the Finnish coalition government said it wanted to "guarantee that Finland fulfil all the convergence criteria" for taking part in EMU.
Currency stability is a criterion for the single currency and some countries argue that the EU's Maastricht Treaty requires countries to be in the ERM to qualify for EMU.
European Commission President Jacques Santer and Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said the Finnish ERM-link would boost the chances of the single currency.
"The enlargement of the mechanism to include a new currency is a very positive signal on the way to the realisation of the euro," they said in a statement.
In Paris, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis hailed the markka link as another sign that the international community was committed to monetary stability.
Officials said the monetary committee, made up of senior finance ministry and central bank officials from the 15 EU member states, had not discussed the Italian lira.
Italy has said it wants to return to the grid this year.
Britain, Sweden and Greece are also outside the grid.
The Finnish markka's central rate of 3.04 against the mark came as no surprise, even if it was trading stronger at 2.986 on Friday.

"Everyone was assuming the markka was going to join soon with a central rate of around 3.03 (per mark) so this is not a huge surprise," said Stephen King, international economist at HSBC markets in London.

The markka will be allowed to fluctuate by up to 15 percent against the other currencies in the grid, the normal margins since the ERM bands were widened in August 1993 after severe pressure on the system.
However, the Bank of Finland will aim for a narrower trading range. "It will certainly be our policy to keep it within a relatively narrow range," Bank of Finland director Matti Vanhala told Reuters.
In Stockholm, the Swedish central bank said Finland's membership would not affect Sweden's position that it does not have to join the ERM to qualify for EMU.
